title: Why no ranking
hookLine: this path teaches schools in their own terms, because each has carried people across
last: SAMAGGI: DIFFERENT IN BODY, ONE IN MIND.

cards: The town is called Kesaputta, and its people, the Kalamas, are tired. Teachers keep passing through. Each one arrives, praises his own teaching, and picks apart everyone else's.
The next does the same, in reverse. So when the Buddha comes through, the Kalamas ask him straight out: we're confused. Which of these people is telling the truth?
It's the perfect moment for him to say: me. He doesn't.

teach.b: First, the test, which you met back in year one.
In the Kalama Sutta, the Buddha says it makes sense that they're unsure, and tells them not to settle it by report, by tradition, by scripture, by clever reasoning, or by the standing of the teacher.

Look at what a teaching does. When you know for yourselves that something leads to greed, hatred and confusion, to harm and suffering, set it aside. When you know it leads to welfare and happiness, take it up.
Second, the raft. In another discourse, the Buddha compares his teaching to a raft. A man faces a wide river, danger on this side and safety on the far side.
He binds a raft from sticks and grass and paddles across. Should he then carry it on his head forever? No.
The teaching is for crossing over, not for holding on to. Third, honest history.
Schools have argued. Some Mahayana texts used a dismissive name for other paths, Hinayana, the lesser vehicle.
Theravada keeps an old book of debates, the Kathavatthu, setting out its answers to views held by other schools. Disagreement is real and long.
That's exactly why this path teaches each school in its own terms, the way its own teachers would explain it, and doesn't pick a winner. Fourth, the reason.

Each of these schools has been a raft. Monks in Thai forests, Zen students in Kyoto, grandmothers chanting in Lhasa, families at a Korean temple: their rafts look different, and people have crossed on all of them.
Ranking the rafts doesn't get anyone across.

how: Buddhist teachers point to the Kalama Sutta's test of a teaching by its fruits and the raft simile's teaching that the dhamma is for crossing over, and inter-school bodies meet without asking anyone to give up their own school.

o: every school taught in its own terms, with no winner picked
a rule that no Buddhist may ever criticize a teacher
the belief that every school teaches exactly the same

s: the Buddha told the Kalamas to trust him because he was the Buddha

games.q: you're the Buddha. the Kalamas ask which of the many teachers is telling the truth. what do you say?
o: trust me: I'm the one who's right.
trust whichever teacher is most well-known.
test a teaching by what it leads to, for yourselves.
games.why: he doesn't name himself the winner. he tells them to look at whether a teaching leads to harm or to welfare.

practice: Bring to mind one school you've met this year that you'll probably never join; maybe its chanting, its rules or its way of sitting isn't your style.
Picture one person it has carried, a nun, a farmer, a grandmother, a teenager in a temple courtyard, reaching the far bank on that raft. Honor it quietly, without needing to climb aboard.

wordCard.voice: Why no ranking. Because each school has carried people across, this path teaches every one in its own terms and picks no winner. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali Kalama: the people of Kesaputta who asked the Buddha whom to believe.

carryVoice: Your line: no ranking. Learning how each raft floats does more than ranking them. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Alagaddupama Sutta (Majjhima Nikaya 22), the raft simile
